demographics: More common in males than females
Higher prevalence in urban and lower-income areas
Use is reported across all socioeconomic and racial groups

risk_factors.text: Peer or social exposure to cocaine use
Other substance use, including alcohol, cannabis, or opioids
History of another substance use disorder
Family history of substance use disorder
Co-occurring psychiatric illness such as depression, anxiety, or ADHD

family_history: Substance use disorder in a first-degree relative
social_history: Current or past cocaine use by snorting, smoking (crack), or injection
Use of other substances, including alcohol, heroin, or cannabis
Injection drug use with shared needles

chief_complaints.text: I feel like my heart is racing and I can't calm down
I've been using cocaine and I want to stop
I feel anxious and jittery after using
I can't sleep and I feel awful when I don't use
My chest hurts and I'm short of breath
I hear voices or feel paranoid

hpi.onset: Acute intoxication effects begin within seconds to minutes of use; chronic use and withdrawal develop over weeks to years
hpi.duration: Intoxication effects last minutes to about an hour; withdrawal symptoms last days to weeks
hpi.progression: Patterns range from occasional recreational use to escalating binge use with tolerance, dependence, and cocaine use disorder; complications such as chest pain, seizures, or psychosis can occur at any point
hpi.location: Systemic; nasal insufflation causes local nasal symptoms, injection causes local skin and vein problems
hpi.radiation: Chest pain may radiate to the arm, jaw, or back if cardiac ischemia is present
hpi.quality: Stimulant effect described as intense energy, euphoria, and alertness, followed by a crash with fatigue, depression, and irritability
hpi.severity: Variable; can range from mild jitteriness to life-threatening complications such as myocardial infarction, stroke, seizure, or hyperthermia
hpi.timing: Effects peak within minutes and fade within an hour; binge patterns involve repeated dosing every few minutes to hours
aggravating: Using larger amounts or more potent routes such as smoking or injecting
Combining with alcohol or other drugs

associated_symptoms.text: Nasal congestion, nosebleeds, or loss of smell with snorting
Chest pain or shortness of breath

pertinent_negatives: Fever with stiff neck or rash suggesting meningitis
Focal weakness or numbness suggesting stroke
Severe headache with sudden onset suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage
Vomiting before the pain in a young patient suggesting appendicitis
Dysuria or flank pain suggesting urinary infection or stones
Recent travel or sick contacts suggesting infection
Prescription stimulant use or ADHD medication

argues_against: Productive cough with fever suggesting pneumonia
Right lower quadrant pain with migration
Sudden focal neurologic deficit suggesting stroke
Primary psychotic disorder without substance use

positives.text: Track marks or scarring at injection sites

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, or cardiac complications rather than euphoria; effects of stimulants are more likely to cause arrhythmias and hypertension.
Use can cause placental abruption, preterm labor, and fetal distress; the patient may present with vaginal bleeding or contractions rather than typical stimulant symptoms.
In young children, accidental exposure or passive inhalation can cause agitation, seizures, or lethargy; they cannot describe the high.
Injection drug use increases risk of serious infections such as endocarditis, abscesses, and pneumonia, which may dominate the presentation.

general.mild: Alert, talkative, mildly restless; pupils enlarged; no distress
general.moderate: Agitated, diaphoretic, pacing, pressured speech, tremulous
general.severe: Markedly agitated, hyperthermic, hypertensive, paranoid, may require restraint
general.critical: Obtunded or comatose, or violently agitated with seizures, hyperthermia, and hemodynamic instability

findings.maneuver: Inspect the pupils in room light and test the pupillary light reflex
findings.finding: Dilated pupils that react sluggishly to light

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal septum and mucosa with a light and speculum
findings.finding: Septal erythema, crusting, perforation, or epistaxis from insufflation

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Regular tachycardia without murmur or gallop

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff
findings.finding: Elevated systolic and diastolic pressure

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate and observe the work of breathing
findings.finding: Rapid shallow breathing without accessory muscle use

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the lungs in all fields
findings.finding: Diffuse expiratory wheezing
Bibasilar crackles suggesting pulmonary edema or aspiration

findings.maneuver: Measure core temperature and inspect the skin for sweating
findings.finding: Elevated temperature with hot, flushed, diaphoretic skin

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms outstretched and observe
findings.finding: Fine postural tremor of the hands

findings.maneuver: Inspect the antecubital fossae, forearms, hands, and feet for injection sites
findings.finding: Needle track marks, scarring, or collapsed veins

findings.maneuver: Palpate any indurated, tender, or fluctuant areas at injection sites
findings.finding: Abscess or cellulitis at an injection site

findings.maneuver: Observe behavior and attempt a calm interview
findings.finding: Psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, poor impulse control

findings.maneuver: Ask about suspiciousness, being watched, or being followed
findings.finding: Paranoid ideation or frank delusions

findings.maneuver: Ask about hearing or seeing things others do not; ask about formication
findings.finding: Auditory or tactile hallucinations, including sensation of bugs under the skin

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength, sensation, and cranial nerves
findings.finding: Focal weakness, numbness, or cranial nerve deficit suggesting stroke

findings.maneuver: Observe for convulsive activity and assess postictal state
findings.finding: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity

findings.maneuver: Test nuchal rigidity and Brudzinski and Kernig signs
findings.finding: No meningismus

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants and percuss the costovertebral angles
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound

labs.caveat: Order in any cocaine user with chest pain, dyspnea, or ECG changes; a single early value can be normal, so repeat at 1-3 hours. Cocaine-associated myocardial infarction can occur with normal coronary arteries.
Marked elevation suggests rhabdomyolysis from agitation, seizures, or hyperthermia; watch for acute kidney injury.
Rises with rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, or hyperthermia.
Hyperkalemia accompanies rhabdomyolysis and renal injury.
Low bicarbonate suggests a metabolic acidosis from seizures, ischemia, or rhabdomyolysis.
Elevated from agitation, seizures, ischemia, or shock.
Hyperglycemia from catecholamine surge; check a bedside glucose in any altered patient to exclude hypoglycemia.
Mild leukocytosis can be stress-related; marked elevation or left shift should prompt a search for infection, especially in injection drug use.
Transaminitis can reflect ischemic hepatitis, rhabdomyolysis, or viral hepatitis in injection drug use.
Hematuria can accompany rhabdomyolysis or renal injury; dipstick blood may be positive from myoglobin.
From poor intake and increased metabolic demand.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or treatment decisions.
Acidemia in severe intoxication with seizures, hyperthermia, or shock.

imaging.preferred_when: Focal neurologic deficit, severe headache, or altered mental status

imaging.study: CT angiography of the head and neck

Chest pain with ECG changes, heart failure, or suspected endocarditis

Valve vegetation in injection drug use

initial.why: Detects ischemia, arrhythmia, and conduction delay in any cocaine user with chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea
Screens for cocaine-associated myocardial infarction; repeat if initially normal and symptoms persist
Assesses electrolytes, renal function, and acid-base status
Looks for leukocytosis suggesting infection, especially in injection drug use
Bedside glucose in any altered or agitated patient to exclude hypoglycemia
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and treatment decisions
Screens for urinary infection and myoglobinuria
Evaluates chest pain, dyspnea, or suspected pneumonia
initial.only_if: chest pain, dyspnea, or fever is present
focal neurologic deficit, severe headache, or altered mental status

confirmatory.why: Detects cocaine metabolite benzoylecgonine; supports recent use but does not establish intoxication or impairment

confirmatory.test: CT angiography of the head and neck
confirmatory.why: Confirms vasospasm, dissection, or large vessel occlusion when stroke is suspected
confirmatory.only_if: focal neurologic deficit or severe headache is present

supporting.why: Detects rhabdomyolysis after agitation, seizures, or hyperthermia
Assesses tissue hypoperfusion or severe agitation
Screens for hepatic injury or ischemic hepatitis
Screens for hepatic injury or ischemic hepatitis
Assesses wall motion and valve function
supporting.only_if: heart failure, murmur, or suspected endocarditis
severe chest pain with widened mediastinum or pulse deficit

not_indicated.why: Not routine in the absence of chest or respiratory symptoms

not_indicated.test: CT angiography of the head and neck

not_indicated.why: Not routine without features of dissection
No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Nonspecific and not needed for the diagnosis of cocaine intoxication

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
ECG within 10 minutes of arrival for chest pain or palpitations
Repeat troponin at 1-3 hours if the first is normal and symptoms persist
Bedside glucose in any patient with altered mental status
Do not delay treatment of agitation, hyperthermia, or seizures for drug testing

differential.name: Acute coronary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm, thrombosis, and increased myocardial demand, so chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis in a user can be a true myocardial infarction rather than just stimulant effect.
differential.trigger: Chest pain, dyspnea, or ECG changes in a cocaine user

history: Chest pressure or heaviness rather than only racing heart
Pain radiating to arm, jaw, or back
Pain with exertion or after a binge
exam: Diaphoresis, pallor, or signs of heart failure
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiogram
ecg: T wave inversions in a coronary distribution

differential.name: Stimulant intoxication from another drug (amphetamine or methamphetamine)
differential.why_considered: Produces the same sympathomimetic toxidrome of tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, agitation, and hyperthermia.

history: Reported use of amphetamines, methamphetamine, or prescription stimulants
Longer duration of effect than cocaine
Access to ADHD medication or diet pills
exam: Similar sympathomimetic findings; may have more prolonged psychosis
Bruxism or skin picking more prominent
labs: Urine drug screen positive for amphetamines, negative for cocaine metabolite

differential.name: Alcohol or sedative-hypnotic withdrawal
differential.why_considered: Can present with tremor, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, and seizures, mimicking stimulant intoxication.
differential.trigger: Tremor, agitation, and autonomic hyperactivity in a patient who stopped heavy drinking

history: Heavy daily alcohol or benzodiazepine use with recent cessation
Prior withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens
Symptoms worse 24-72 hours after last drink
exam: Coarse tremor, tongue fasciculations, or hallucinosis
Normal or small pupils rather than dilated
labs: Elevated AST and ALT with AST greater than ALT

differential.name: Serotonin syndrome
differential.why_considered: Causes agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia, tremor, and clonus, overlapping with severe cocaine toxicity.
differential.trigger: Recent serotonergic medication plus agitation, hyperthermia, and clonus

history: Recent start or dose increase of an SSRI, SNRI, MAOI, tramadol, or triptan
Symptoms began after medication change
exam: Lower extremity rigidity greater than upper

differential.name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.why_considered: Presents with hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status, which can resemble severe cocaine intoxication.
differential.trigger: Recent antipsychotic or dopamine antagonist use with lead-pipe rigidity and high fever

history: Recent antipsychotic, antiemetic, or dopamine antagonist exposure
Symptoms developing over days

differential.name: Thyroid storm
differential.why_considered: Causes tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation, and tremor, mimicking stimulant toxicity.

history: Known Graves disease or thyroid disease
Recent illness, surgery, or infection
Weight loss, heat intolerance, and diarrhea over weeks
labs: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 or T3

differential.name: Pheochromocytoma
differential.why_considered: Episodic catecholamine release causes paroxysmal hypertension, palpitations, sweating, and anxiety.

history: Episodic spells with headache, palpitations, and sweating
Spells triggered by pressure, micturition, or exercise
No drug use
exam: Hypertension during spells, may be normal between episodes
labs: Elevated plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine metanephrines
imaging: Adrenal mass on CT or MRI

differential.name: Sepsis or meningitis
differential.why_considered: Fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and altered mental status can overlap with cocaine intoxication, especially in injection drug users.
differential.trigger: Fever with leukocytosis or meningismus in an injection drug user

history: Fever and chills
Recent infection or indwelling line
Headache and neck stiffness
exam: Meningismus, focal neurologic deficit, or rash
imaging: Meningeal enhancement on CT or MRI

differential.name: Primary psychotic disorder
differential.why_considered: Paranoia, hallucinations, and agitation can be caused by cocaine but may also represent a primary psychiatric illness.

history: Psychotic symptoms predating drug use
Symptoms persist during prolonged abstinence
Family history of schizophrenia
exam: Formal thought disorder, negative symptoms, or bizarre delusions
No sympathomimetic signs such as mydriasis or tachycardia
labs: Urine drug screen negative for cocaine

severity.mild: Alert and talkative with mild restlessness, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and elevated blood pressure; no chest pain, neurologic deficit, or hyperthermia.
severity.moderate: Agitated, diaphoretic, tremulous, and hypertensive with pressured speech; may have vomiting, headache, or mild hyperthermia but no end-organ damage.
severity.severe: Marked agitation, hyperthermia, severe hypertension, paranoia, hallucinations, or seizures; risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, or rhabdomyolysis.
severity.critical: Coma, status epilepticus, malignant hyperthermia, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock, aortic dissection, or intracerebral hemorrhage; requires immediate resuscitation.

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with ST changes or rising troponin
red_flags.meaning: Cocaine-associated myocardial infarction; needs aspirin, benzodiazepines, nitrates, and cardiology involvement

red_flags.finding: Focal neurologic deficit or severe sudden headache
red_flags.meaning: Stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, or subarachnoid hemorrhage; urgent noncontrast head CT

red_flags.finding: Temperature above 104 F (40 C) with rigidity
red_flags.meaning: Hyperthermia from severe intoxication; risk of rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, and death
Severe toxicity or withdrawal; may indicate intracranial hemorrhage or metabolic derangement

red_flags.finding: Systolic blood pressure above 180 or diastolic above 120 with symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Hypertensive emergency; risk of aortic dissection, stroke, or myocardial infarction

red_flags.finding: Agitation requiring restraint or violent behavior
red_flags.meaning: Risk of injury to patient and staff; treat with benzodiazepines and avoid antipsychotics if possible

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or bradycardia in a known cocaine user
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a mixed ingestion such as speedball, sepsis, or cardiogenic shock rather than pure stimulant effect

complications.name: Cocaine-associated myocardial infarction
clues: Chest pain during or shortly after use
ST elevation or depression on ECG

complications.name: Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke
clues: Sudden focal weakness, numbness, or aphasia

complications.name: Hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis
clues: Dark urine and elevated creatine kinase

complications.name: Aortic dissection
clues: Pulse deficit or blood pressure difference between arms

complications.name: Cocaine-induced psychosis
clues: Symptoms resolving with abstinence and sedation

complications.name: Infective endocarditis
clues: Fever, new murmur, or embolic phenomena in an injection drug user

complications.name: Cocaine use disorder and dependence
clues: Continued use despite health, legal, or social consequences

special_populations.differences: Cocaine causes placental abruption, preterm labor, fetal growth restriction, and fetal distress; presentation may be vaginal bleeding or contractions rather than typical stimulant symptoms. Avoid cocaine and manage obstetric emergencies urgently.
Accidental ingestion or passive inhalation can cause agitation, seizures, lethargy, or apnea; children cannot report euphoria. Supportive care and poison control consultation are key.
May present with confusion, falls, arrhythmias, or myocardial infarction rather than euphoria; underlying coronary disease and hypertension increase complication risk.
Rhabdomyolysis and dehydration can precipitate acute kidney injury; monitor creatine kinase, creatinine, and urine output closely.
Cocaine is metabolized by the liver; hepatic impairment may prolong effects and increase toxicity. Also screen for viral hepatitis in injection users.
Injection drug use increases risk of serious infections such as endocarditis, abscesses, and pneumonia, which may dominate the presentation.

key_questions.question: What substances have you been using, and how do you take them?
key_questions.looking_for: Cocaine by snorting, smoking (crack), or injection; also alcohol, heroin (speedball), or other stimulants

key_questions.question: When did you last use, and how much did you use?
key_questions.looking_for: Use within minutes to hours; binge pattern with repeated dosing; larger amounts or more potent routes

key_questions.question: How long do the effects last for you?
key_questions.looking_for: Minutes to about an hour, shorter than amphetamines; helps separate cocaine from other stimulants

key_questions.question: Do you feel like your heart is racing, or is your chest hurting?
key_questions.looking_for: Palpitations, chest pressure or heaviness, dyspnea, or diaphoresis suggesting cardiac ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you had any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or a sudden severe headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic deficit or thunderclap headache suggesting stroke, hemorrhage, or vasospasm

key_questions.question: Any shaking spells, passing out, or muscle twitching?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, tremor, or rigidity suggesting severe toxicity or withdrawal

key_questions.question: How has your mood and sleep been, especially when you are not using?
key_questions.looking_for: Crash with depression, fatigue, increased appetite, bad dreams, insomnia, and slowed thinking

key_questions.question: Have you needed more cocaine to get the same effect, or tried to cut down and couldn't?
key_questions.looking_for: Tolerance, cravings, loss of control, and continued use despite consequences (cocaine use disorder)

key_questions.question: Do you hear voices or feel that people are watching or following you?
key_questions.looking_for: Paranoia, auditory or tactile hallucinations, or formication suggesting cocaine-induced psychosis

key_questions.question: Do you snort, smoke, or inject? Do you share needles or equipment?
key_questions.looking_for: Route-specific complications: nasal damage, respiratory symptoms, track marks, abscesses, HIV or hepatitis C risk

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or new rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Infection such as endocarditis, abscess, or pneumonia, especially in injection drug use

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which changes imaging and treatment decisions and raises risk of abruption and preterm labor

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including any stimulants for ADHD or diet pills?
key_questions.looking_for: Prescription stimulants, serotonergic drugs, or antipsychotics that could explain the findings

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had problems with drugs or alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of substance use disorder

key_questions.question: Have you ever been told you have depression, anxiety, or another mental health condition?
key_questions.looking_for: Co-occurring psychiatric illness that may predate or complicate cocaine use

key_questions.question: Any allergies to medications?
key_questions.looking_for: Allergies that affect choice of sedatives, analgesics, or antibiotics

reasoning_points: Reported or suspected cocaine use by snorting, smoking, or injection, often with a binge pattern
Sympathomimetic toxidrome: tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, agitation, diaphoresis, and hyperthermia
Rapid onset within minutes and short duration of effect, distinguishing cocaine from amphetamines
Route-specific findings such as nasal septal damage, track marks, or respiratory symptoms
Complications considered and excluded: myocardial infarction, stroke, seizure, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and psychosis
Urine drug screen positive for the cocaine metabolite benzoylecgonine supports recent use

Look-alikes considered: other stimulant intoxication, alcohol or sedative withdrawal, serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, thyroid storm, pheochromocytoma, sepsis or meningitis, and primary psychotic disorder
Pregnancy status checked before imaging and treatment decisions
Cocaine use disorder assessed through tolerance, cravings, loss of control, and continued use despite consequences

easy: Young adult with reported cocaine use and classic sympathomimetic findings
Racing heart, dilated pupils, agitation, and hypertension after use
Nasal congestion, nosebleeds, or septal irritation from snorting
Urine drug screen positive for cocaine metabolite
medium: Chest pain with ECG changes requiring troponin testing and cardiac workup
Paranoia or hallucinations that could be cocaine-induced or a primary psychotic disorder
Injection drug user with fever and a new murmur suggesting endocarditis
Tremor, agitation, and tachycardia that could be alcohol or sedative withdrawal
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion, falls, or arrhythmia rather than euphoria
Pregnant patient with vaginal bleeding or contractions from placental abruption
Hyperthermia with rigidity and elevated creatine kinase mimicking neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome
Mixed ingestion such as speedball with hypotension or bradycardia instead of pure stimulant effect
Child with accidental exposure presenting with agitation, seizures, or lethargy and no reported use
